Clarke opens with the title. The Hebrew for degrees derives from a verb meaning to go up, whence steps or stairs, though some have applied it to elevation of voice and others to the excellence of the matter, so that Junius and Tremellius prefixed to each the label of a most excellent ode. Kimchi reported fifteen temple steps on each of which one of these fifteen songs was sung, an opinion Clarke traces into an apocryphal gospel, though he answers that no such steps or practices can be proved. He judges instead that the collection was sung by the returning exiles going up to Jerusalem, doubts that any one hand made them, and lists the six names to which they have been ascribed without evidence. Augustine reads the degrees as a ladder used both ways: some climb toward the understanding of spiritual things, others come down to the infants to say what infants can take, that after milk they may grow strong enough for solid meat. Delitzsch joins this song to the last verse of the psalm before it, whose writer likens himself to a straying sheep, and calls this poet a sheep among wolves; he leaves the period open, noting a proposal that these songs belong to the years after the Return, when Samaritan hostility tried to keep the young colony down.

Calvin will not affirm the authorship but finds David's manner throughout, and takes the chief purpose to be a complaint of how Saul's flatterers bent all their ingenuity on his destruction; the opening thanksgiving he reads as deliberate encouragement to others, since though men need help every moment, no season is fitter for seeking it than when danger is immediately upon them. Spurgeon measures the wound: slander is sharper than the sword, rousing indignation by its injustice while leaving us helpless, for a cutlass can be parried but nothing shields against a liar's tongue, and one cannot learn who fathered the falsehood or where it has travelled. He advises silence toward men and prayer toward God, since stirring the matter spreads it and appealing to the traducers' honour is as useless as pleading with wolves.

Henry divides the injury in two. They told lies to David, professing friendship so as to carry their designs unsuspected, smiling and kissing while aiming to smite under the fifth rib; and they told lies of him, laying to his charge things he never knew. He adds that a man who had prayed to be kept from lying himself might the more confidently pray not to be belied by others. Gill traces the same lips through Doeg, Saul's courtiers, the Pharisees, the hail of Judas and the false witnesses. Ellicott generalizes it to the nation: of all that embittered Israel under foreign rule, taunts and calumny cut deepest and scarred longest.

The arrows and the coals then divide them. Ellicott reads the third verse rhetorically, taking the subject as indefinite, so that the question is what further epithet could be added to a tongue already called lying and false, and the answer supplies the two stock figures of malicious speech, the whetted arrow and fire, both here elaborated. Calvin reports that some make the fourth verse a description of calumny and others the punishment awaiting it, and takes it himself as comparison, slander piercing like an arrow and burning long like these coals. Gill allows the first reading but prefers the second, and Henry and Wesley take it flatly as the wrath of God, Henry observing that the sinner sets God at a distance but that arrows reach from afar. On the coals themselves Gill and Henry both repeat the report that they hold fire a full year; Ellicott corrects the plant to broom, notes that Arabs uproot it for charcoal of the finest quality, and treats the year-old embers as one of the wonderful stories told by Jerome and the rabbis.
5:
Nobody thinks the psalmist lived in both places. The Moschi lay between the Black and Caspian seas, Kedar in the Arabian desert, and dwelling among both at once is impossible. Ellicott turns that objection into the argument for the pairing: the remoteness is the point, one savage people fetched from the north and one from the south as poetry dictated, and he allows that the poet may have needed to veil an allusion to real and powerful tribes. Gill hesitates, reporting that some make the sons of Meshech the Muscovites and Scythians and the Targum the Asiatics, but preferring the Cappadocians on the authority of Josephus, since Kedar lay nearer Judea. Clarke keeps them geographical, following Calmet in placing Meshech in the mountains between Iberia and Armenia, subdued by Nebuchadnezzar and holding Jewish exiles, while Kedar reached toward the Euphrates and became the country of the Saracens.

Henry and Wesley cut the knot. David never lived in either country, Henry says; he lived among people as rude as their inhabitants, exactly as we say of bad neighbours that we dwell among Turks and heathens, and Wesley adds that the names are to be taken metaphorically since the next verse explains them. Calvin argues the case at length and reaches the same place by a different road. He insists the word is a proper name against the ancient versions, which render it as an appellative so that the complaint becomes one of protracted exile; but having fixed the name, he holds that under it the psalmist means his own countrymen, dishonoured by the borrowed title of nations whose cruelty the Jews knew well, and observes drily that we still call gross and ignorant people by the names of distant nations. Though David was living in his own land, Calvin says, he was a stranger in it.

What follows they take as the explanation. Calvin makes the psalmist now point with the finger at those he had marked out indirectly, perfidious Israelites wearing the mask rather than bearing the seed of Israel. Henry guesses that Saul's court was the Meshech and Kedar meant, and notes that a good man is grieved twice over, at the distance from the ordinances of God, since he is never at home while banished from them, and at the company he is held in, like Lot in Sodom, among neighbours who are thorns. Gill turns the sixth verse into a chain: those who hate peace hate the God of peace, the Prince of peace, the sons of peace, the Gospel of peace and the way of peace, and are like the troubled sea that cannot rest. Clarke keeps it concrete, describing a restless marauding people who live in tents and subsist by robbery, with the captives wishing them to take up the arts of peace while they would hear of nothing but their old manner of life.

The last verse is agreed in substance and pressed hardest by Henry and Calvin. The Hebrew says simply "I peace," which Gill renders as being wholly peace, a man devoted to it who follows it with all men; Henry expands it into a portrait, a man who will part with anything in reason for peace and who spoke reason and love only to hear the answer "To arms." Calvin adds that speaking here amounts to offering terms, so that the enemies' refusal to speak at all shows how brutal their pride was, since they disdained a man who had never injured them; and he draws the lesson that abstaining from injury is not enough, for the faithful must study to win others by gentleness and then wait in patience. Henry sees Christ in it: for his love they were his adversaries, and for his good works they stoned him. Ellicott, whose note here is a fragment, records only the pregnant force of the two-word Hebrew.
